p:cNvPr.descr: Two illustrations and a graph show the steps and results in site-directed mutagenesis. (a)The far left diagram shows the steps in site-directed mutagenesis (labeled above). The diagram begins with a recombinant vector (labeled right) at the top, which is a ring with a green top half and a yellow bottom half. Below is a down arrow with a gray text box to the right reading, “Cleave with restriction endonuclease.” Below, the recombinant vector has cleaved at two places on the green half. The cracks are visible, but the pieces have not yet been removed. Two small arrows point to the cleavage sites. Below this is a down arrow with a convergent arrow on the left showing the addition of a green fragment with a thin red line down the center; this is labeled “mutation.” To the right is a gray text box reading, “Insert synthetic DNA segment containing mutation.” Below this is the recombinant vector, now with the thin red mutation line down the middle of its green section on top. (b) To the right, a diagram showing the process of oligonucleotide-directed mutagenesis (labeled above). The diagram begins with a blue plasmid, which consists of two blue rings arranged in concentric circles. On the left are two green areas, slightly thicker than the plasmid rings, labeled, “Gene, target site for mutation.” Below this is a down arrow with a convergent arrow on the left showing the addition of primers, which are two small, curved orange segments with an X in the center of each. To the right is a gray text box that reads, “Denature plasmid and anneal oligonucleotide primers with mutation.” Below is an image of the two plasmid rings separated, with the larger ring on the left and the smaller ring on the right. Each still has the green gene segment, and each has an orange primer to its left, right beside the green gene segment. Below is a down arrow with a gray text box to the left reading, “Use DNA polymerase to extend and incorporate the mutagenic primers.” Below, the left larger blue plasmid has the primer inside it. A yellow arrow begins at the bottom end of the primer and follows the inside of the plasmid all the way around to the left. To the right, the smaller blue plasmid has the primer on the outer left side, with a yellow arrow coming out of the top of the primer, all the way around the outside of the plasmid to the right. The yellow arrows are synthetic DNA copies of the plasmid. A down arrow below has a text box to the right reading, “Digest nonmutated parental DNA template with methylation-specific nuclease, and anneal newly synthesized strands.” Below, the plasmid rings are now yellow, representing the new synthetic DNA strands. They are arranged as two concentric circles, with the orange primer sections attached at the left side, one to the outside circle and one to the inside circle. To the left, pointing to the primers, is text reading, “Mutated plasmid with nicked strands”. To the bottom, a down arrow points to a text box reading, “Transform dsDNA into cells. Cell repairs nicks in mutated plasmid.” (c) To the right are two graphs from an automatic sequencer showing a nucleotide sequence with multicolored peaks. At the top is a graph labeled, “Wild-type recA.” The top horizontal axis is labeled with the following nucleotide sequence: TCTTCCGGTAAAACCACGC. The first three As in the sequence are shaded pink. The peaks have colors corresponding to the nucleic acids. T is represented by yellow, C by red, G by green, and A by blue. They are arranged in peaks according to their appearance in the sequence. The bottom graph is labeled, “Mutant recA K72R.” This time the sequence at the top horizontal axis of the graph is TCTTCCGGTCGCACCACGC. The CGC portion is shaded light pink and the letters are in red, to show the mutation. The peaks in this graph are considerably lower and the peaks correspond to the presence in the sequence.
